key_insight: The paper operationalises the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis by introducing "task complexity" — the length of the shortest program that attains a target performance — enabling quantitative tests of whether fine-tuning merely surfaces pre-trained knowledge or requires new learning.
problem_solved: The Superficial Alignment Hypothesis lacked a precise, testable definition, leading to conflicting arguments and critiques; this work provides a concrete metric to compare tasks and evaluate claims about what is learned during pre-training versus post-training.
method: Define task complexity as the minimal-program-length (algorithmic) description that achieves a target performance on a task, framing SAH in terms of program-length gaps between pre-training and fine-tuning.
Develop practical approximations for task complexity (e.g., compressibility, program-synthesis or model-based proxies) so the metric can be estimated on real tasks and models.
Empirically evaluate the metric across a suite of tasks and model settings to test SAH predictions (correlating estimated task complexity with fine-tuning gains and transfer behavior).
impact: Provides practitioners a quantitative tool to predict when fine-tuning will simply surface pre-trained capabilities versus when it must induce new algorithmic structure, informing dataset design, transfer expectations, and allocation of compute for pre-training vs fine-tuning.
visual_elements: Concept diagram: shortest-program / Kolmogorov-style illustration showing low vs high task complexity (short vs long program).
Scatter plot: estimated task complexity (x-axis) vs fine-tuning improvement or required fine-tuning compute (y-axis) to show correlation patterns.
Pipeline flowchart: pre-training → task complexity estimation (proxy methods) → fine-tuning & evaluation → SAH verdict.
Icons/comparisons: side-by-side examples of low-complexity tasks (surfaceable) and high-complexity tasks (requiring new learning) with brief captions.
paper_title: Operationalising the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis via Task Complexity
paper_authors: Tomás Vergara-Browne, Darshan Patil, Ivan Titov, Siva Reddy, Tiago Pimentel
